share.messagePlain: Europe needs a night train from {origin} to {destination}. Here's what it would take:
share.emailBody: This is what a {origin} – {destination} night train would look like — route, timetable and running costs, modelled on the Back-on-Track Target Network:

targetNetwork.fact: Europe ran about 100 night train lines in 2025 — roughly what you are planning here.
targetNetwork.demand: 300 lines by 2035, enough to triple the number of night train passengers.

sevenInTen.fact: 7 in 10 Europeans say they would take a night train instead of a plane, given reasonable conditions.
sevenInTen.demand: dominant booking platforms to be required to show every night train running in their country.

euEmissions.fact: A comprehensive European night train network could avoid 3% of the EU's total greenhouse gas emissions.
euEmissions.demand: the Connecting Europe Facility — nearly €40 billion over six years — to co-finance night train coaches and track access charges.

aviation.fact: Moving travellers from planes to night trains could cut about a quarter of aviation emissions.
aviation.demand: a minimum airline ticket price, to stop fares being dumped below cost.

climate.fact: Taking a night train is about 30 times better for the climate than flying the same route.
climate.demand: VAT scrapped on international rail tickets — international flights are already taxed at 0%.

europeanSleeper.fact: European Sleeper's Brussels–Berlin–Prague route carried more than 230,000 passengers on over 750 trains in its first year.
europeanSleeper.demand: the EU to buy sleeper and couchette coaches and lease them out, so newcomers like this one carry less risk.

flyLess.fact: Nearly half of surveyed night train passengers say they will fly less and take the train more over the next five years.
flyLess.demand: night trains prioritised when train paths are allocated, so the services people want can actually run.

carpatia.fact: Since December 2025 the Carpatia sleeper has linked Przemyśl and Kraków with Vienna, Salzburg and Munich.
carpatia.demand: EU co-funding for pilot routes to Europe's edges — Portugal, Greece, the Nordics, the Baltics.

parisBerlin.fact: A Paris–Brussels–Berlin sleeper has run since March 2026, and Brussels–Milan is due to follow.
parisBerlin.demand: closed border stations reopened — no passenger train has crossed between Irun and Hendaye since 2020.

rollingStock.fact: Europe has roughly 1,500 night train carriages. A full network needs several thousand more by 2035.
rollingStock.demand: the European Investment Bank's Green Rail Investment Platform actually funded — the budget line is still empty.

reuse.fact: About 1,300 publicly funded carriages are being scrapped in France, while Europe is short of sleeper stock.
reuse.demand: EU rules that make reusing second-hand rolling stock possible instead.

network.fact: Back-on-Track is a volunteer network of around 60 active members, with groups in eleven European countries.
network.demand: night trains treated as their own transport segment, exempt from track access surcharges.

schedule.title: Schedule
schedule.caption: days per week, by month
schedule.info: How often the train runs in each month of the year, and what follows from it. Operating days are the days in each month times its days per week, so the evaluation year has 366 days — 2032 is a leap year. Departures are operating days times two directions; train-km and place-km follow from the route length and the formation. Which weekday the train runs is not modelled. The fleet is sized to the busiest month: a rake needs the cycle length in days, so a train that runs seven days a week and takes two days to come back needs two rakes.
schedule.dragHint: Drag a column, or use the arrow keys.
schedule.previewHint: Departures, train-km, places and place-km follow from the grid; trainsets use the cycle of {cycle} days, which only a recalculation can redo. Recalculate to apply the schedule to every other panel.
schedule.previewHintNoCycle: Departures, train-km, places and place-km follow from the grid. The trainset count needs the cycle length from a calculation — recalculate to fill it in.

prices.title: Places and prices
prices.caption: {composition} · {places} places
prices.info: What the train offers and what it charges. The tariff is three parts, each per class. The BASE FARE has a fixed term and a distance term — a berth has a price of admission a short journey pays as surely as a long one, so pricing on distance alone made short connections implausibly cheap. ADDITIONAL SERVICES is the revenue from bicycles, oversized luggage and reservations sold with the ticket; it is ordinary ticket revenue, never negative, and it carries overhead and the profit requirement like any other fare. CATERING is the odd one: one signed NET figure per passenger, the restaurant’s own sales less its own costs, and therefore outside those two bases. It differs by class because the classes differ in what their base fare already includes. The two example columns price the BERTH only — fixed plus distance — over the longest and shortest journey the route sells. Demand does not respond to any of it yet: the demand model is a stopgap.
prices.weightedAverage: average per passenger, weighted by places

operation.compareInfo: Every composition in the catalogue, evaluated on THIS route under the selected scenario — so the figures are comparable with each other and with nothing else. Trainsets first: it is the first thing that changes when the schedule does. The two density columns are metres and tonnes per place, the physical price of comfort; they replace the catalogue's indicative unit costs, which said the same thing about every route.
operation.selectedInfo: The composition the figures on this page were computed with. Below it, what one trip costs to run, in three receipts: the rakes and their upkeep, the locomotive hours, and the people on board. Fleet euros are annual breakdown leaves divided by the year's departures; locomotive and staff euros are per single trip, because the two directions differ in running time and in where the duty boundaries fall.
operation.onePairOfMany: figures for one trip pair of several

tac.title: Track access charges
tac.info: What each infrastructure manager charges for the run over its network, country by country. The "charged on" column lists the terms that country actually levies on this trip — distance (at the day rate, or partly at the night rate where the country has a night band and the trip falls in it), gross weight, places, a fixed per-kilometre add-on, stop fees, a share of revenue, a congestion surcharge — and leaves out the ones it does not. A crossing billed by its own operator is a separate line. The outbound trip is shown; the two directions can differ where a night band catches one and not the other.
tac.strip: Track access charges, from one trip

stations.title: Station access charges
stations.info: One charge per stop call, levied by the station's own infrastructure manager at that country's rate. Every stop of the trip is a call, the terminals included.
stations.strip: Station access, from one trip ({cycle} stop events per cycle, {year} per year)

facilities.title: Service facilities — parking
facilities.info: Stabling the formation between arrival and the next departure, at each arrival terminal, on the basis that country prices — per metre and started day, per started hour, or per event — after its free allowance, plus the power drawn while standing. Priced per operating day, one stay per location; the per-trip line is one stay averaged over both ends.
facilities.caption: one stay per terminal per operating day
facilities.perTripRow: Per trip — one stay, averaged over both ends
facilities.none: No stabling priced on this route.

energy.title: Energy
energy.info: Traction energy for the run, country by country: the kWh the train draws over that country's kilometres, priced at the country's tariff — a flat rate, or a day and a night rate where the country has a night band, with the share drawn inside it — plus the catenary charge where one is levied. All figures are net of VAT; the model carries no VAT rate.

year.title: Infrastructure per year
year.info: The four infrastructure leaves of the cost breakdown, per year, each with its cost per train-kilometre and its share of the infrastructure total. These are the same figures the Costs and revenue section reports under Infrastructure.

infrastructure.defaultLegend: marks a figure priced from the EU-average default because the country or stop has no value of its own.

overhead.cateringOutside: Catering ({value} per trip) is outside: it is a net figure, its own overhead already inside it.
overhead.marginNote: Deducted in the net result — not a cost paid to anyone.

variable.title: Variable overhead
variable.covers: Covers sales, distribution and customer service.
variable.info: The operator's selling costs, charged as a share of ticket revenue rather than of the full cost — that is how the model defines them. Catering is outside the base: the contribution is already net of the restaurant's own sales, costs and overhead, so charging distribution overhead on it would count the same overhead twice.
variable.caption: a share of ticket revenue

fixed.title: Fixed overhead
fixed.info: The operator's running of itself, charged as a share of its OTHER operating costs. Two things are outside that base on purpose: variable overhead, which is already an overhead, and the infrastructure charges, which are paid to somebody else and are not the operator's to administer.
fixed.caption: a share of the operator's other costs

margin.title: Expected margin
margin.info: The operating profit the operator is expected to keep, as a share of ticket revenue. It is not a cost anybody receives — it is subtracted in the net result, which is why a route can need a subsidy while every bill is paid. Catering is outside this base too, for the same reason it is outside the overhead base.
margin.caption: a share of ticket revenue
margin.covers: The operating profit the operator is expected to keep. Not a cost paid to anyone.

overhead.fixedBaseItems: Staff, locomotive lease, coach maintenance, on-board service, coach amortisation, financing, cleaning, shunting. Not in it: variable overhead, and everything paid to infrastructure managers.

demand.title: Demand
demand.caption: interim assumption, per year
demand.info: What the interim demand assumption produces. Passengers are the places actually sold — the figure the catering contribution multiplies — not the placeholder trip count the KPI grid shows. Ticket revenue and the catering contribution are listed separately because they are earned in different ways and one of them can be negative.
demand.restsOnInfo: The demand side of the model is a stopgap. Every figure on this tab is replaced once a real demand model lands; nothing here is a prediction.
demand.whenItLands: When the demand model lands, this tab shows demand by connection, by class and by the mode each passenger shifted from — and the prices under Supply get elasticities.

gallery.heading: It's time to bring night trains back on track!

welcome.pitch: We at Back on Track are currently developing our proposal for a Target Network 2032 — a night train network of around 300 connections spanning the continent, doubling the current number of connections. This tool is a way for anyone with an interest in night trains to support our mission: suggest the night train of your dreams for us to incorporate in our Target Network proposal!
